title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) to quantify the marginal benefit of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) relative to accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a seeded deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and produced a single shared generator output per intent (shared_initial_generation) evaluated in both arms. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...). Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 for all guarded episodes). We release the complete preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...), raw model/provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...), and analysis artifacts for exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect given the specific task/model/validator combination and discuss implications for future confirmatory designs that seek to demonstrate verifier and repair utility in operationally realistic settings.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a high‑value NetOps use case: it promises faster change cycles and lower manual effort but carries risk because incorrect or out‑of‑sequence changes can cause reachability regressions or outages. A widely advocated architecture to mitigate that risk is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): a generator (LLM) produces a candidate configuration, a verifier (emulator/validator) checks properties (reachability, group membership, ordering constraints), and an automated repair step attempts to fix violations. Numerous systems and position works recommend this pattern because it separates stochastic generation from deterministic checking and correction and enables auditable, bounded changes. Yet the marginal operational benefit of adding a verifier+repair layer depends on the generator error profile, the validator’s coverage and fidelity, and the task distribution. Absent preregistered control, claims that verifiers reduce regressions are vulnerable to selection and analysis degrees of freedom.
To produce a reproducible causal estimate of verifier marginal effect we designed a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment. Key design decisions frozen before data collection: (1) deterministic task sampling from a public synthetic pool; (2) single shared generator output per task that both arms evaluate (shared_initial_generation); (3) a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and fixed repair policy allowing at most one repair call per guarded episode; and (4) a single requested_model (gpt-5-mini) with a strict max‑call budget. The primary estimand was the paired difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded minus baseline). All decisions, seeds, and analysis workflows were preregistered (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) and all run artifacts were cryptographically hashed and archived (e.g., master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d...).
Contributions. (i) A fully preregistered, paired, artifact‑grounded execution comparing G→V→R to LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks with per‑episode validator traces. (ii) Complete publicizable provenance: model/provider traces, responses, scoring traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts with exact SHA‑256 values to enable exact replay. (iii) A transparent empirical outcome and interpretation: under the chosen task/model/validator regime the verifier had no marginal effect because generator proposals satisfied the validator in every case; we document the ceiling case and provide concrete design guidance for future confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM assistance for NetOps/AIOps has several strands: intent translation, configuration synthesis, and closed‑loop agentic workflows that use verifiers and repair loops. Recent benchmarks and systems (e.g., Cornetto and other generate→validate→repair pipelines) emphasize formal verification or emulation to detect regressions at scale and report that verifier guidance can reduce regressions when generators err. Position arguments recommend restricting LLMs to translation/translation‑to‑model tasks while relying on solvers/identical determiners for long‑horizon reasoning and safety; others propose evolving verifiers or hybrid agentic stacks that combine LLMs with deterministic solvers. We located and verified the most relevant literature leads that motivated our design (see cited_record_ids). Our study departs from prior work by preregistering a strict paired design holding the generator output fixed and by publishing the entire artifact chain: this isolates the marginal verifier effect without conflating generator variability, a design choice that complements prior work focused on end‑to‑end agentic workflows or multi‑model leaderboards.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory framing. The procedure and analysis were frozen in the preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 in execution manifest). Primary hypothesis H1: the G→V→R pipeline yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only pipeline (paired estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The power plan targeted an absolute reduction of 0.08 assuming baseline regression rate ≈ 0.20 (two‑sided α=0.05, power=0.80); sensitivity scans across baseline rates were preregistered. The preregistration mandated deterministic sampling, deterministic validator semantics, one shared generator call per task, and a one‑repair‑call cap if guarded validation failed.
Task generation, deterministic sampling, and inclusion rules. Tasks originated from a public synthetic task pool produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. To guarantee replayability and avoid human selection bias we applied the following deterministic selection: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, take the first K=200 tasks after filtering to those for which the preregistered validator reported coverage. All selection steps and exclusions were automatically logged; no human adjudication occurred post‑lock. Each task manifest entry recorded: the task_payload (initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow constraints), generation_seed, and the exact required_sequence used to parse validator expectations; examples and representative entries are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 f1d447b7...).
Shared initial generation and paired design. For each task we performed a single generator call (shared_initial_generation) to produce candidate configuration candidate_c. The baseline arm treated candidate_c as the suggested apply; the guarded arm ran the deterministic validator on candidate_c, and—only if the validator flagged a violation—could invoke a single preregistered repair call to the same model to attempt correction (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This design isolates verifier marginal effect by holding generator output identical across arms. The total planned episodes = 2 × K = 400; provider model call budget maximum_model_calls = 400. Actual model_calls_used = 200 because the shared generation covered both arms per task.
Validator semantics, scoring, and repair policy. The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parses candidate configuration text into structured commands and enforces preregistered dependency and workflow checks (examples: shutdown before MTU change, minimum‑up group constraints, protected interface invariants). The primary scoring rule for the confirmatory outcome was full_intent_constraint_validation; scoring traces record normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshot, violation_codes, and valid boolean. When valid==false the repair policy permits one automated repair invocation with a constrained repair prompt; repaired candidate is revalidated once. All scoring outputs were archived under execution/scoring/*.json (representative hashes provided in the execution manifest). Repair instrumentation recorded repair_applied flags and repair prompt hashes; in this run repair_applied == false for all guarded episodes.
Model and provider configuration. The requested_model was gpt-5-mini recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 1acce92558ed...). Provider call traces and per‑call hashing were archived for each shared_initial_generation (execution/provider_calls/*.json). Per‑call caching metadata and call_cache entries were preserved to detect inadvertent cross‑condition reuse; auditing confirmed no cross‑condition cache reuse for this run (deterministic_reconciliation.json).
Statistical analysis plan. Confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (apply passed validator or not). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples and seed=1729 (as preregistered); we also recorded the paired contingency table n11,n10,n01,n00. Secondary estimands (time to deploy, model calls per successful apply) were preregistered but became moot because repair was never invoked; all analysis artifacts and logs were archived (analysis/* with SHA‑256 hashes documented).

Repair pathway and operational cost accounting. The guarded policy’s repair pathway was never triggered for any task: repair_applied=false across all execution/scoring/*.json traces (example execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 3055f874...). Because validation returned valid==true for every shared candidate there were no blocked applies and no observable latency differences attributable to repair attempts. Representative per‑task traces (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) show normalized_response equaling normalized_reference_answer and validator.violation_count == 0.

All per‑episode validator final_state snapshots and normalized_configuration strings are archived to support independent replay and to enable external revalidation of the scoring rule.
sections.discussion:
Null outcome interpretation and ceiling effect. The observed degenerately null outcome—perfect validator compliance in both arms—arises because, for the sampled task pool and the chosen generator (gpt-5-mini) and validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), the generated candidate configurations satisfied all preregistered validator constraints. Under the shared_initial_generation paired design this implies the verifier never observed a failing candidate and therefore had no opportunity to change the binary apply outcome. The result is a valid and informative ceiling case: it documents a regime where G→V→R, as instantiated, yields no marginal benefit.
Design implications for future confirmatory studies. Demonstrating verifier/repair utility in a confirmatory framework requires a failure‑rich evaluation design. Practical recommendations grounded in our artifacts: (1) sample task pools with higher baseline error propensity—include intents that deliberately probe validator boundary conditions or include partially covered features; (2) evaluate weaker or multiple generator models to produce a nonzero baseline error rate; (3) include adversarial or perturbed generator outputs to force verifier engagement; or (4) change estimand to measure generator‑verifier feedback benefits by allowing iterative generator responses to verifier feedback (a generative‑interactive design). Our preregistered shared_initial_generation design deliberately isolates verifier marginal effect but prevents generator adaptation to verifier feedback—explicitly: the shared initial generation design intentionally forbids the generator from receiving verifier feedback and thus precludes observing benefits that arise from a reactive generator.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: preserved via deterministic sampling, seed logging, and cryptographic hashing of artifacts (execution/* SHA values). Construct validity: the primary outcome measures validator.valid; whether validator.valid corresponds to operationally meaningful regression avoidance depends on validator fidelity. External validity: limited by single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and by restricting to validator‑covered intents; the run therefore does not generalize to production distributions or other model families. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (target baseline=0.20) were violated because observed baseline = 1.0; in such situations statistical power analyses based on the assumed baseline are not informative. We therefore present exact tests and bootstrap CIs and avoid overinterpreting nullity.
Operational implications. For practitioners the finding indicates that, under certain benign task/model regimes, a verifier may be unnecessary because generator proposals are already compliant; however, production NetOps environments have far richer and noisier distributions, vendor idiosyncrasies, and stateful interactions that our synthetic validator may not capture. Therefore operators should not infer from this ceiling case that verifiers are redundant in real deployments. Instead, the artifacts show how to design reproducible evaluation contracts that diagnose when verifiers will matter: a task bank that intentionally samples near the verifier boundary or that includes historical failure cases is required to observe concrete verifier benefits.
Reproducibility and artifact use. Every material decision and per‑episode artifact is archived with a SHA‑256 hash; critical artifacts and their hashes are listed in the execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 3dfbe1b6..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 1acce925..., preregistration SHA‑256 a6d73a5c..., master prompt SHA‑256 1872df1e...). Researchers wishing to replay the experiment can (i) retrieve the deterministic task generator and task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 f1d447b7...), (ii) reproduce the single shared generation per task using the same requested_model and the archived shared_initial_provider_call traces, and (iii) replay validation via the archived execution/scoring/*.json validator traces. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms internal accounting and provider call audit consistency.
Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed. We explicitly report the preregistered power assumptions (target baseline failure = 0.20; target absolute reduction = 0.08) and show observed baseline = 1.0 to make the design mismatch immediate to readers. We also add an explicit statement that shared_initial_generation prevents generator adaptation to verifier feedback and that an alternate interactive generator–verifier design could yield different operational outcomes. Both clarifications are supported by the preregistration and execution artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, paired, artifact‑grounded evaluation comparing G→V→R against an LLM‑only acceptance policy on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks. Under the specific task/model/validator regime the verifier had no marginal effect: both arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked. This outcome demonstrates a ceiling case and underscores the necessity—when evaluating verifier/repair value—of selecting task/model combinations where baseline generator error is nontrivial or of intentionally sampling verifier boundary cases. We release the full artifact bundle (preregistration, execution traces, scoring, and analysis artifacts) to enable exact replay and to inform future preregistered evaluations that seek to quantify verifier and repair utility in more operationally realistic settings.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
